Spatial tensor products: complete proof supplement through the commutation theorem

Original text by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), September 2026; public domain (CC0). Scoped selection and prerequisite bindings by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026; original contributions CC0. The mathematical text of the selected proofs is retained.

Sections 1–11 give the complete construction of spatial tensor products and the tensor commutation theorem. Hilbert spaces and orthogonal families can have arbitrary cardinality. Countable vector series describe one normal functional and impose no separability hypothesis.

The proofs use Hilbert completion, projection and Riesz representation over the real and complex fields, bounded adjoints, continuous functional calculus and positive-functional Cauchy–Schwarz. Their full published providers are the Hilbert-space, continuous-calculus and GNS chapters of Foundations of von Neumann algebras. Section 4 supplies its own bicommutant proof.

For Theorem 10.1(3), use the published Kaplansky chapter, Theorem 7.1, and the published trace-class/predual chapter, Theorem 9.4(a). For Theorem 10.1(4), use the bounded normal-functional support proof in the universal-enveloping chapter, “State and support tools used below” and Lemma 11.1. For the comments following Corollaries 8.3–8.4, the universal-enveloping chapter, Corollary 11.4, proves normality of isomorphisms; the tensor-isomorphism proof itself explicitly tensors the given normal inverse. These four incoming statements are full proofs in the published foundation reader.

Section 11 proves tensor commutation by real orthogonal complements and cyclic corners. General Tomita–Takesaki theory, standard-form modular implementers, weights and semifiniteness are not prerequisites of this proof.

Conventions

Hilbert spaces are complex. Inner products are linear in the first variable. No separability or dimension condition is imposed anywhere, and the zero space is allowed. A sum over an arbitrary index set is the limit of the net of its finite partial sums. Every Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis.

B(H)B(H)B(H) is the algebra of bounded operators on HHH. For ξ,η∈H\xi,\eta\in Hξ,η∈H put ωξ,η(x)=⟨xξ,η⟩\omega_{\xi,\eta}(x)=\langle x\xi,\eta\rangleωξ,η​(x)=⟨xξ,η⟩ and ωξ=ωξ,ξ\omega_\xi=\omega_{\xi,\xi}ωξ​=ωξ,ξ​. For a set S⊆B(H)S\subseteq B(H)S⊆B(H), S′S'S′ is its commutant. It is a unital algebra, closed in the weak operator topology, and a ∗*∗-algebra when S∗=SS^*=SS∗=S. We call a ∗*∗-algebra M⊆B(H)M\subseteq B(H)M⊆B(H) with M′′=MM''=MM′′=M a von Neumann algebra on HHH. It contains 111 and is weakly closed. On the zero space, B(0)={0}B(0)=\{0\}B(0)={0} is a von Neumann algebra.

3. Normal functionals and the amplification

The ultraweak topology. Let B(H)∗B(H)_*B(H)∗​ be the set of functionals ρ(x)=∑n⟨xξn,ηn⟩,∑n∥ξn∥2<∞,∑n∥ηn∥2<∞,(3.1) \rho(x)=\sum_n\langle x\xi_n,\eta_n\rangle,\qquad \sum_n\|\xi_n\|^2<\infty,\quad \sum_n\|\eta_n\|^2<\infty , \tag{3.1} ρ(x)=n∑​⟨xξn​,ηn​⟩,n∑​∥ξn​∥2<∞,n∑​∥ηn​∥2<∞,(3.1) with countable or finite index sets. A square-summable family of any size has only countably many nonzero members, so larger index sets give nothing new. The series converges absolutely, and ∣ρ(x)∣≤∥x∥ (∑∥ξn∥2)1/2(∑∥ηn∥2)1/2|\rho(x)|\leq\|x\|\,(\sum\|\xi_n\|^2)^{1/2}(\sum\|\eta_n\|^2)^{1/2}∣ρ(x)∣≤∥x∥(∑∥ξn​∥2)1/2(∑∥ηn​∥2)1/2. B(H)∗B(H)_*B(H)∗​ is a linear space: merge two families to add, and scale one sequence to multiply by a scalar. The ultraweak topology, also called the σ\sigmaσ-weak topology, is the weakest topology in which every ρ∈B(H)∗\rho\in B(H)_*ρ∈B(H)∗​ is continuous. It is finer than the weak operator topology, so every weakly closed set, in particular every commutant, is ultraweakly closed.

A linear map Φ\PhiΦ from a subspace of B(H)B(H)B(H) to B(L)B(L)B(L) is normal if it is ultraweakly continuous, that is, if ρ∘Φ\rho\circ\Phiρ∘Φ is ultraweakly continuous for every ρ∈B(L)∗\rho\in B(L)_*ρ∈B(L)∗​. For a subspace Y⊆B(H)Y\subseteq B(H)Y⊆B(H), Y∗Y_*Y∗​ denotes its normal functionals. Compositions of normal maps are normal. For fixed A∈B(L,L′)A\in B(L,L')A∈B(L,L′) and C∈B(L′,L)C\in B(L',L)C∈B(L′,L), the map X↦AXCX\mapsto AXCX↦AXC from B(L)B(L)B(L) to B(L′)B(L')B(L′) is normal, since ∑n⟨AXCζn,ζn′⟩=∑n⟨X(Cζn),A∗ζn′⟩\sum_n\langle AXC\zeta_n,\zeta_n'\rangle=\sum_n\langle X(C\zeta_n),A^*\zeta_n'\rangle∑n​⟨AXCζn​,ζn′​⟩=∑n​⟨X(Cζn​),A∗ζn′​⟩. For positive maps, normality is often expressed instead through suprema of bounded increasing nets; part (3) of the next proposition gives this order form for the amplification.

Proposition 3.1.

  1. (Normal functionals.) Let Y⊆B(H)Y\subseteq B(H)Y⊆B(H) be any linear subspace. A linear functional on YYY is ultraweakly continuous if and only if it is the restriction of some ρ∈B(H)∗\rho\in B(H)_*ρ∈B(H)∗​. In particular, every normal functional on YYY is bounded.
  2. (Normality of the amplification.) The map a↦a⊗1Ka\mapsto a\otimes1_Ka↦a⊗1K​, B(H)→B(H⊗K)B(H)\to B(H\otimes K)B(H)→B(H⊗K), is a unital ∗*∗-homomorphism. It is isometric if K≠0K\ne0K=0 and zero if K=0K=0K=0. It is normal: for ρ=∑nωζn,ζn′∈B(H⊗K)∗\rho=\sum_n\omega_{\zeta_n,\zeta_n'}\in B(H\otimes K)_*ρ=∑n​ωζn​,ζn′​​∈B(H⊗K)∗​, ρ(a⊗1)=∑n∑j⟨aRj∗ζn,Rj∗ζn′⟩,∑n,j∥Rj∗ζn∥2=∑n∥ζn∥2,(3.2) \rho(a\otimes1)=\sum_{n}\sum_j\langle aR_j^*\zeta_n,R_j^*\zeta_n'\rangle,\qquad \sum_{n,j}\|R_j^*\zeta_n\|^2=\sum_n\|\zeta_n\|^2 , \tag{3.2} ρ(a⊗1)=n∑​j∑​⟨aRj∗​ζn​,Rj∗​ζn′​⟩,n,j∑​∥Rj∗​ζn​∥2=n∑​∥ζn​∥2,(3.2) so ρ( ⋅⊗1)∈B(H)∗\rho(\,\cdot\otimes1)\in B(H)_*ρ(⋅⊗1)∈B(H)∗​. 4. The bicommutant theorem and the normal extension principle

Lemma 4.1 (amplified density). Let A⊆B(H)A\subseteq B(H)A⊆B(H) be a ∗*∗-subalgebra with 1∈A1\in A1∈A, and let x∈A′′x\in A''x∈A′′. So P∈(A⊗1)′P\in(A\otimes1)'P∈(A⊗1)′. By the commutation criterion (2.1), every matrix entry PjkP_{jk}Pjk​ lies in A′A'A′. As x∈A′′x\in A''x∈A′′, xxx commutes with every PjkP_{jk}Pjk​, and Proposition 2.1(3) shows that x⊗1x\otimes1x⊗1 commutes with PPP. Since 1∈A1\in A1∈A, ζ∈E\zeta\in Eζ∈E, so (x⊗1)ζ=P(x⊗1)ζ∈E(x\otimes1)\zeta=P(x\otimes1)\zeta\in E(x⊗1)ζ=P(x⊗1)ζ∈E. Choose a∈Aa\in Aa∈A with ∥((x−a)⊗1)ζ∥<ε\|((x-a)\otimes1)\zeta\|<\varepsilon∥((x−a)⊗1)ζ∥<ε. By the column expansion (1.2), the square of the left side is ∑n∥(x−a)ξn∥2\sum_n\|(x-a)\xi_n\|^2∑n​∥(x−a)ξn​∥2. □\square□

Theorem 4.2 (bicommutant theorem). For a ∗*∗-subalgebra A⊆B(H)A\subseteq B(H)A⊆B(H) with 1∈A1\in A1∈A, A′′A''A′′ is the closure of AAA in the strong, the weak and the ultraweak topology. A ∗*∗-subalgebra that contains 111 and is closed in one of these topologies is a von Neumann algebra.

Proof. Strong density is Lemma 4.1 for finite families. For ultraweak density, let x∈A′′x\in A''x∈A′′ and ρ1,…,ρm∈B(H)∗\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_m\in B(H)_*ρ1​,…,ρm​∈B(H)∗​ with ρi=∑nωξni,ηni\rho_i=\sum_n\omega_{\xi^i_n,\eta^i_n}ρi​=∑n​ωξni​,ηni​​. Then ∣ρi(x−a)∣≤(∑n∥(x−a)ξni∥2)1/2(∑n∥ηni∥2)1/2|\rho_i(x-a)|\le(\sum_n\|(x-a)\xi^i_n\|^2)^{1/2}(\sum_n\|\eta^i_n\|^2)^{1/2}∣ρi​(x−a)∣≤(∑n​∥(x−a)ξni​∥2)1/2(∑n​∥ηni​∥2)1/2 is small for all iii at once. Conversely, A′′A''A′′ is weakly closed and the weak topology is coarser than the other two, so each closure of AAA lies in A′′A''A′′. The last sentence follows. □\square□

The general form of the theorem, for ∗*∗-subalgebras that need not contain 111, is proved in the lesson The double commutation theorem. The unital case is all we need.

Proposition 4.3 (normal extension principle). Let MMM be a von Neumann algebra on HHH, A⊆MA\subseteq MA⊆M a ∗*∗-subalgebra with 1∈A1\in A1∈A and A′′=MA''=MA′′=M, and Φ,Ψ:M→B(L)\Phi,\Psi:M\to B(L)Φ,Ψ:M→B(L) normal linear maps.

  • (i) If Φ=Ψ\Phi=\PsiΦ=Ψ on AAA, then Φ=Ψ\Phi=\PsiΦ=Ψ.
  • (ii) If P⊆B(L)P\subseteq B(L)P⊆B(L) is a von Neumann algebra and Φ(A)⊆P\Phi(A)\subseteq PΦ(A)⊆P, then Φ(M)⊆P\Phi(M)\subseteq PΦ(M)⊆P.
  • (iii) Let S⊆MS\subseteq MS⊆M be a self-adjoint set with S′′=MS''=MS′′=M, and let Φ,Ψ\Phi,\PsiΦ,Ψ be ∗*∗-homomorphisms. If Φ(S)⊆P\Phi(S)\subseteq PΦ(S)⊆P and Φ(1)∈P\Phi(1)\in PΦ(1)∈P, then Φ(M)⊆P\Phi(M)\subseteq PΦ(M)⊆P. If Φ=Ψ\Phi=\PsiΦ=Ψ on S∪{1}S\cup\{1\}S∪{1}, then Φ=Ψ\Phi=\PsiΦ=Ψ.

Proof. (i) Let ρ∈B(L)∗\rho\in B(L)_*ρ∈B(L)∗​. The functional ρ∘(Φ−Ψ)\rho\circ(\Phi-\Psi)ρ∘(Φ−Ψ) is normal on MMM. By Proposition 3.1(1) it is the restriction of some σ=∑nωξn,ηn∈B(H)∗\sigma=\sum_n\omega_{\xi_n,\eta_n}\in B(H)_*σ=∑n​ωξn​,ηn​​∈B(H)∗​, and σ\sigmaσ vanishes on AAA. For x∈Mx\in Mx∈M and a∈Aa\in Aa∈A, ∣σ(x)∣=∣σ(x−a)∣≤(∑n∥(x−a)ξn∥2)1/2(∑n∥ηn∥2)1/2|\sigma(x)|=|\sigma(x-a)|\le(\sum_n\|(x-a)\xi_n\|^2)^{1/2}(\sum_n\|\eta_n\|^2)^{1/2}∣σ(x)∣=∣σ(x−a)∣≤(∑n​∥(x−a)ξn​∥2)1/2(∑n​∥ηn​∥2)1/2, which Lemma 4.1 makes arbitrarily small. So ρ(Φ(x))=ρ(Ψ(x))\rho(\Phi(x))=\rho(\Psi(x))ρ(Φ(x))=ρ(Ψ(x)) for every ρ\rhoρ, in particular for every vector functional, and Φ(x)=Ψ(x)\Phi(x)=\Psi(x)Φ(x)=Ψ(x).

(ii) For p′∈P′p'\in P'p′∈P′, the map x↦Φ(x)p′−p′Φ(x)x\mapsto\Phi(x)p'-p'\Phi(x)x↦Φ(x)p′−p′Φ(x) is normal and vanishes on AAA. By (i) it vanishes on MMM. So Φ(M)⊆P′′=P\Phi(M)\subseteq P''=PΦ(M)⊆P′′=P.

(iii) Let AAA be the span of 111 and all finite products of elements of SSS. It is a ∗*∗-subalgebra containing 111 and SSS, and A′=S′A'=S'A′=S′, so A′′=S′′=MA''=S''=MA′′=S′′=M. Since Φ\PhiΦ is a ∗*∗-homomorphism and PPP is a unital ∗*∗-algebra, Φ(A)⊆P\Phi(A)\subseteq PΦ(A)⊆P; in the second case Φ=Ψ\Phi=\PsiΦ=Ψ on AAA. Apply (ii) and (i). □\square□

For example, let GGG be a locally compact group with left regular representation λ\lambdaλ. The set S=λ(G)S=\lambda(G)S=λ(G) is self-adjoint, because λ(g)∗=λ(g−1)\lambda(g)^*=\lambda(g^{-1})λ(g)∗=λ(g−1), and it contains 1=λ(e)1=\lambda(e)1=λ(e). 5. The spatial tensor product

Definition 5.1. Let M⊆B(H)M\subseteq B(H)M⊆B(H) and N⊆B(K)N\subseteq B(K)N⊆B(K) be von Neumann algebras. M⊙NM\odot NM⊙N is the linear span of the operators x⊗yx\otimes yx⊗y with x∈Mx\in Mx∈M, y∈Ny\in Ny∈N. By Proposition 2.1(1) it is a ∗*∗-subalgebra of B(H⊗K)B(H\otimes K)B(H⊗K) containing 111. The spatial tensor product is M⊗ˉN=(M⊙N)′′,(5.1) M\bar\otimes N=(M\odot N)'' , \tag{5.1} M⊗ˉ​N=(M⊙N)′′,(5.1) the smallest von Neumann algebra that contains every x⊗yx\otimes yx⊗y. For sets S⊆B(H)S\subseteq B(H)S⊆B(H) and T⊆B(K)T\subseteq B(K)T⊆B(K) we write S⊗1={s⊗1:s∈S}S\otimes1=\{s\otimes1:s\in S\}S⊗1={s⊗1:s∈S} and 1⊗T={1⊗t:t∈T}1\otimes T=\{1\otimes t:t\in T\}1⊗T={1⊗t:t∈T}.

Theorem 5.2.

  1. (Closure.) M⊗ˉNM\bar\otimes NM⊗ˉ​N is a von Neumann algebra on H⊗KH\otimes KH⊗K. It is the closure of M⊙NM\odot NM⊙N in the strong, the weak and the ultraweak topology. In particular it is strongly closed.
  2. (Generators.) If S⊆B(H)S\subseteq B(H)S⊆B(H) and T⊆B(K)T\subseteq B(K)T⊆B(K) are self-adjoint sets with S′′=MS''=MS′′=M and T′′=NT''=NT′′=N, then M⊗ˉN=(S⊗1∪1⊗T)′′M\bar\otimes N=(S\otimes1\cup1\otimes T)''M⊗ˉ​N=(S⊗1∪1⊗T)′′. In particular M⊗ˉN=(M⊗1∪1⊗N)′′M\bar\otimes N=(M\otimes1\cup1\otimes N)''M⊗ˉ​N=(M⊗1∪1⊗N)′′.
  3. (Bounded strong limits.) Let (Xα)(X_\alpha)(Xα​) be a bounded net in B(H⊗K)B(H\otimes K)B(H⊗K), let X∈B(H⊗K)X\in B(H\otimes K)X∈B(H⊗K), and let D⊆H⊗KD\subseteq H\otimes KD⊆H⊗K be a total set with Xαζ→XζX_\alpha\zeta\to X\zetaXα​ζ→Xζ for every ζ∈D\zeta\in Dζ∈D. Then Xα→XX_\alpha\to XXα​→X strongly. If every XαX_\alphaXα​ lies in M⊗ˉNM\bar\otimes NM⊗ˉ​N, so does XXX. One may take D={ξ⊗η:ξ∈D1, η∈D2}D=\{\xi\otimes\eta:\xi\in D_1,\ \eta\in D_2\}D={ξ⊗η:ξ∈D1​, η∈D2​} for total sets D1⊆HD_1\subseteq HD1​⊆H, D2⊆KD_2\subseteq KD2​⊆K.
  4. (Amplification.) For every set S⊆B(H)S\subseteq B(H)S⊆B(H), (S⊗1)′′=S′′⊗1(S\otimes1)''=S''\otimes1(S⊗1)′′=S′′⊗1. Hence M⊗1M\otimes1M⊗1 is a von Neumann algebra, M⊗ˉC1K=M⊗1M\bar\otimes\mathbb C1_K=M\otimes1M⊗ˉ​C1K​=M⊗1 and C1H⊗ˉN=1⊗N\mathbb C1_H\bar\otimes N=1\otimes NC1H​⊗ˉ​N=1⊗N. The map x↦x⊗1x\mapsto x\otimes1x↦x⊗1 is a normal unital ∗*∗-homomorphism of MMM onto M⊗1⊆M⊗ˉNM\otimes1\subseteq M\bar\otimes NM⊗1⊆M⊗ˉ​N. It is injective and isometric when K≠0K\ne0K=0.
  5. (Matrices over MMM.) With matrices as in Proposition 2.1(2), M⊗ˉB(K)={X∈B(H⊗K):Xjk∈M for all j,k}=(M′⊗1)′,(5.2) M\bar\otimes B(K)=\{X\in B(H\otimes K):X_{jk}\in M\ \text{for all }j,k\}=(M'\otimes1)', \tag{5.2} M⊗ˉ​B(K)={X∈B(H⊗K):Xjk​∈M for all j,k}=(M′⊗1)′,(5.2) and B(H)⊗ˉB(K)=B(H⊗K)B(H)\bar\otimes B(K)=B(H\otimes K)B(H)⊗ˉ​B(K)=B(H⊗K).

Proof. (1) By (5.1), M⊗ˉNM\bar\otimes NM⊗ˉ​N is the double commutant of a self-adjoint set, hence a von Neumann algebra. The rest is the bicommutant theorem (Theorem 4.2) with A=M⊙NA=M\odot NA=M⊙N.

(2) By the commutation criterion (2.1), (S⊗1)′(S\otimes1)'(S⊗1)′ consists of the operators whose entries lie in S′=S′′′=M′S'=S'''=M'S′=S′′′=M′. So (S⊗1)′=(M⊗1)′(S\otimes1)'=(M\otimes1)'(S⊗1)′=(M⊗1)′. Rows give (1⊗T)′=(1⊗N)′(1\otimes T)'=(1\otimes N)'(1⊗T)′=(1⊗N)′. Hence (S⊗1∪1⊗T)′=(M⊗1∪1⊗N)′(S\otimes1\cup1\otimes T)'=(M\otimes1\cup1\otimes N)'(S⊗1∪1⊗T)′=(M⊗1∪1⊗N)′. The last set equals (M⊙N)′(M\odot N)'(M⊙N)′, because M⊗1M\otimes1M⊗1 and 1⊗N1\otimes N1⊗N lie in M⊙NM\odot NM⊙N and x⊗y=(x⊗1)(1⊗y)x\otimes y=(x\otimes1)(1\otimes y)x⊗y=(x⊗1)(1⊗y). Take commutants.

(3) Let C=sup⁡α∥Xα∥+∥X∥C=\sup_\alpha\|X_\alpha\|+\|X\|C=supα​∥Xα​∥+∥X∥. Convergence holds on the span of DDD by linearity. Given ζ\zetaζ and ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0, pick ζ0\zeta_0ζ0​ in that span with ∥ζ−ζ0∥<ε\|\zeta-\zeta_0\|<\varepsilon∥ζ−ζ0​∥<ε. Then ∥(Xα−X)ζ∥≤∥(Xα−X)ζ0∥+Cε\|(X_\alpha-X)\zeta\|\le\|(X_\alpha-X)\zeta_0\|+C\varepsilon∥(Xα​−X)ζ∥≤∥(Xα​−X)ζ0​∥+Cε, so lim sup⁡α∥(Xα−X)ζ∥≤Cε\limsup_\alpha\|(X_\alpha-X)\zeta\|\le C\varepsilonlimsupα​∥(Xα​−X)ζ∥≤Cε. The second claim follows from (1), since M⊗ˉNM\bar\otimes NM⊗ˉ​N is strongly closed. The third follows from the totality of product vectors (Proposition 1.3(1)).

(4) If K=0K=0K=0, all sets involved are {0}\{0\}{0}. Let K≠0K\ne0K=0. By (2.1), (S⊗1)′(S\otimes1)'(S⊗1)′ contains 1⊗B(K)1\otimes B(K)1⊗B(K), whose matrix entries are scalars. So (S⊗1)′′⊆(1⊗B(K))′=B(H)⊗1(S\otimes1)''\subseteq(1\otimes B(K))'=B(H)\otimes1(S⊗1)′′⊆(1⊗B(K))′=B(H)⊗1 by Proposition 2.1(4). Now let x∈B(H)x\in B(H)x∈B(H). If x∈S′′x\in S''x∈S′′, then xxx commutes with the entries of every X∈(S⊗1)′X\in(S\otimes1)'X∈(S⊗1)′, since they lie in S′S'S′; by Proposition 2.1(3), x⊗1x\otimes1x⊗1 commutes with XXX. If conversely x⊗1∈(S⊗1)′′x\otimes1\in(S\otimes1)''x⊗1∈(S⊗1)′′, then it commutes with c⊗1c\otimes1c⊗1 for every c∈S′c\in S'c∈S′, so xc=cxxc=cxxc=cx and x∈S′′x\in S''x∈S′′. Thus (S⊗1)′′=S′′⊗1(S\otimes1)''=S''\otimes1(S⊗1)′′=S′′⊗1. For S=MS=MS=M this says (M⊗1)′′=M⊗1(M\otimes1)''=M\otimes1(M⊗1)′′=M⊗1. Applying Proposition 2.1(4) with H=CH=\mathbb CH=C gives {1K}′′=B(K)′=C1K\{1_K\}''=B(K)'=\mathbb C1_K{1K​}′′=B(K)′=C1K​; so (2) with T={1}T=\{1\}T={1} gives M⊗ˉC1=(M⊗1)′′=M⊗1M\bar\otimes\mathbb C1=(M\otimes1)''=M\otimes1M⊗ˉ​C1=(M⊗1)′′=M⊗1, and symmetrically for NNN. The remaining claims are the normality of the amplification (Proposition 3.1(2)) and the norm identity of Proposition 2.1(1).

(5) The entries of x⊗yx\otimes yx⊗y are multiples of xxx, so M⊙B(K)⊆C:={X:Xjk∈M}M\odot B(K)\subseteq\mathcal C:=\{X:X_{jk}\in M\}M⊙B(K)⊆C:={X:Xjk​∈M}. By (2.1), C=(M′⊗1)′\mathcal C=(M'\otimes1)'C=(M′⊗1)′, the commutant of a self-adjoint set; so C′′=C\mathcal C''=\mathcal CC′′=C and M⊗ˉB(K)⊆CM\bar\otimes B(K)\subseteq\mathcal CM⊗ˉ​B(K)⊆C. Conversely, for X∈CX\in\mathcal CX∈C the truncations (2.2) lie in M⊙B(K)M\odot B(K)M⊙B(K), are bounded by ∥X∥\|X\|∥X∥ and converge strongly to XXX. By (3), X∈M⊗ˉB(K)X\in M\bar\otimes B(K)X∈M⊗ˉ​B(K). For M=B(H)M=B(H)M=B(H) we have M′=C1M'=\mathbb C1M′=C1 and (C1⊗1)′=B(H⊗K)(\mathbb C1\otimes1)'=B(H\otimes K)(C1⊗1)′=B(H⊗K). □\square□

Part (3) is how membership in a tensor product is usually proved in practice: one exhibits a norm-bounded net in M⊙NM\odot NM⊙N that converges on a total set of test vectors. Example 12.2 does this for a discrete group, and the end of Section 12 describes the same argument for a locally compact group. Without the norm bound, convergence on a total set does not give strong convergence (Example 5.5). Part (2) allows generating sets that are not von Neumann algebras themselves. For instance, let GGG be a locally compact group, mmm the multiplication representation of L∞(G)L^\infty(G)L∞(G) on L2(G)L^2(G)L2(G), and λ\lambdaλ the left regular representation. Exercise 9.3 (slices by a functional that is not normal). Let N=ℓ∞(N)N=\ell^\infty(\mathbb N)N=ℓ∞(N) on ℓ2(N)\ell^2(\mathbb N)ℓ2(N), and let ω\omegaω be a state of NNN that vanishes on every finitely supported sequence, for instance the limit along a free ultrafilter. Let M⊆B(H)M\subseteq B(H)M⊆B(H) with H≠0H\ne0H=0. Show that ι⊗ω:M⊗ˉN→M\iota\otimes\omega:M\bar\otimes N\to Mι⊗ω:M⊗ˉ​N→M is positive, unital and of norm one, but not normal.

Solution. By Theorem 9.2(1) and (2), ι⊗ω\iota\otimes\omegaι⊗ω is positive, has norm ∥ω∥=1\|\omega\|=1∥ω∥=1, and (ι⊗ω)(1)=ω(1)1=1(\iota\otimes\omega)(1)=\omega(1)1=1(ι⊗ω)(1)=ω(1)1=1. The projections pn=1{1,…,n}p_n=1_{\{1,\ldots,n\}}pn​=1{1,…,n}​ increase strongly to 111, ω(pn)=0\omega(p_n)=0ω(pn​)=0 and ω(1)=1\omega(1)=1ω(1)=1. A normal functional is continuous for the strong topology on bounded sets: write it as in (3.1) and use dominated convergence, as in the proof of Proposition 3.1(2). So ω\omegaω is not normal. By the converse in Theorem 9.2(3), ι⊗ω\iota\otimes\omegaι⊗ω is not normal.

Applied to x(1−e)x(1-e)x(1−e) and (1−e)x(1-e)x(1−e)x, the first condition gives ψ(x)=ψ(xe)=ψ(ex)\psi(x)=\psi(xe)=\psi(ex)ψ(x)=ψ(xe)=ψ(ex). A positive normal ψ\psiψ is faithful exactly when s(ψ)=1s(\psi)=1s(ψ)=1.

Theorem 10.1. Let M⊆B(H)M\subseteq B(H)M⊆B(H) and N⊆B(K)N\subseteq B(K)N⊆B(K) be von Neumann algebras, φ∈M∗\varphi\in M_*φ∈M∗​ and ω∈N∗\omega\in N_*ω∈N∗​.

Part (4) is the "Fubini" description of the tensor product. It is the usual route to statements like W∈L∞(G)⊗ˉL(G)W\in L^\infty(G)\bar\otimes L(G)W∈L∞(G)⊗ˉ​L(G) for a multiplicative unitary WWW. The bounded strong limits of Theorem 5.2(3) give another route, which needs neither the commutation theorem nor any countability; Example 12.2 follows it.

Exercise 11.6 (factors without the commutation theorem). Let M1⊆B(H1)M_1\subseteq B(H_1)M1​⊆B(H1​) and M2⊆B(H2)M_2\subseteq B(H_2)M2​⊆B(H2​) be factors, with H1,H2≠0H_1,H_2\ne0H1​,H2​=0. Show, without the commutation theorem, that M1⊗ˉM2M_1\bar\otimes M_2M1​⊗ˉ​M2​ is a factor.

Solution. This is the argument of B. Blackadar, Operator Algebras, III.1.5.10. Let ZZZ be the centre of M1⊗ˉM2M_1\bar\otimes M_2M1​⊗ˉ​M2​. Then ZZZ commutes with M1⊗1M_1\otimes1M1​⊗1, which lies in the algebra, and with M1′⊗1M_1'\otimes1M1′​⊗1, which lies in its commutant. So the von Neumann algebra Z′Z'Z′ contains ((M1∪M1′)⊗1)′′=(M1∪M1′)′′⊗1((M_1\cup M_1')\otimes1)''=(M_1\cup M_1')''\otimes1((M1​∪M1′​)⊗1)′′=(M1​∪M1′​)′′⊗1, by Theorem 5.2(4). As M1M_1M1​ is a factor, (M1∪M1′)′=M1′∩M1=C1(M_1\cup M_1')'=M_1'\cap M_1=\mathbb C1(M1​∪M1′​)′=M1′​∩M1​=C1, so (M1∪M1′)′′=B(H1)(M_1\cup M_1')''=B(H_1)(M1​∪M1′​)′′=B(H1​). Likewise Z′⊇1⊗B(H2)Z'\supseteq1\otimes B(H_2)Z′⊇1⊗B(H2​). By Theorem 5.2(2) and (5), Z′Z'Z′ contains B(H1)⊗ˉB(H2)=B(H1⊗H2)B(H_1)\bar\otimes B(H_2)=B(H_1\otimes H_2)B(H1​)⊗ˉ​B(H2​)=B(H1​⊗H2​). Hence Z⊆B(H1⊗H2)′=C1Z\subseteq B(H_1\otimes H_2)'=\mathbb C1Z⊆B(H1​⊗H2​)′=C1.

Exercise 11.7 (maximal abelian subalgebras). Let Ak⊆MkA_k\subseteq M_kAk​⊆Mk​ be von Neumann subalgebras with Ak′∩Mk=AkA_k'\cap M_k=A_kAk′​∩Mk​=Ak​ (k=1,2k=1,2k=1,2).
